Journalists should have no legal protections beyond those of any other citizen, and should be fully answerable in court for every false claim they publish and every law they break to get a story.

Government should leave disease prevention entirely to individuals and their doctors, with no mandates, routine population screening programs, or health surveillance.

Voting should be limited to in-person ballots cast on election day by voters who show photo identification and have proven their eligibility in advance, with mail ballots only for those who cannot physically attend.
extra: argument: An election only settles who governs if the losing side can trust that every ballot came from an eligible voter acting freely, and in-person voting with identification is the method that makes that visible.

text: Voting rules should be judged one at a time, keeping any step that measurably protects the count while making sure every eligible citizen has a practical way to meet it.
extra: argument: Both turning away eligible voters and letting doubts about the count grow damage an election, so each rule should be weighed by what it costs in lost votes against what it buys in confidence.

text: Every eligible citizen should be able to vote by whatever method suits them, by mail, early, or in person, with no rule kept in place unless it is shown to stop real wrongdoing without turning away honest voters.

A country should rely on itself as fully as it can, producing what it needs at home, admitting very few newcomers, and joining no body whose rules or courts can bind it.
extra: argument: A country that depends on no one cannot be pressured by trading partners or outside institutions, so its people alone decide how they live.

text: Whether a country should open itself further or rely more on itself depends on its size, its population trends, and the terms on offer, so no single answer fits every nation.
extra: argument: Countries differ so much in their neighbors, their labor needs, and their sense of shared identity that the same level of openness can help one and harm another.

text: A country should open itself as fully as it can to the wider world, with free trade, free movement of people, and full membership in shared institutions that make rules together.

Regions should have no law-making power of their own, and every key decision about them, from shared resources to economic policy, should be made by the national government.
extra: argument: A country whose regions set their own rules breaks into competing interests, and only one national authority can share costs and benefits fairly across all of them.

text: Whether a region should govern itself depends on the issue, because some decisions belong with the region and others belong with the nation.
extra: argument: Problems differ in size, so the right level of government for a decision is the one whose area matches the area the problem actually covers.

text: Regions should have broad self-government over their own economies and public services, while the national government keeps defense and currency.
extra: argument: People in a region know their own needs better than a distant national government, and leaders who answer to regional voters are easier to hold accountable for results.

Government works best when decisions are made as close as possible to the people they affect.
A nation is stronger and fairer when its key decisions are made once, for everyone, by the national government.

City governments should leave nearly all decisions about land, streets, and growth to residents, businesses, and private agreements, and should not add new rules, fees, or plans to steer how a city works.
extra: argument: The people who live, build, and trade in a city know their own needs better than any planning office, and every new rule or fee adds cost and delay that falls on them.

The past should always be presented entirely on its own terms, and no monument, textbook or history should be judged or changed to suit present-day moral standards.

Human remains and sacred objects should never be dug up, kept, or displayed without the consent of the descendant communities or source countries they belong to, and everything already taken should be returned.
extra: argument: The dead and their sacred things belong to the people who claim them as their own, and no scholarly interest outweighs a community's right to decide what happens to its ancestors.

text: Decisions about digging, keeping, and returning finds should be made case by case, weighing what a find can teach against the claims of descendant communities and source countries.
extra: argument: Both the knowledge a find can give and the claims of the people tied to it are real, so any fixed rule either way will get some cases badly wrong.

Sadness, worry, and stress are ordinary parts of life that people should handle through relationships, habits, and their own effort, and treating them as medical conditions does more harm than good.
extra: argument: People who are told their struggles are illnesses come to see themselves as broken and stop trusting their own ability to recover, which is the very ability they most need.

text: Some mental struggles are ordinary hardships best met with personal effort and support from others, while others are real conditions that need professional treatment, and the right response depends on how severe and lasting the problem is.
extra: argument: Matching the response to the severity of the problem spares mild cases from needless treatment while making sure serious cases are not left to fend for themselves.

text: Mental struggles such as depression and anxiety are medical conditions, and anyone who has them should be treated by trained professionals rather than left to manage on their own.
extra: argument: An illness that weakens the will and judgment a person would need to fix it cannot reliably be fixed by that same person's effort, so outside expert care is the only dependable path.

Government should leave production, prices, wages, and trade entirely to free markets and private choice, limiting itself to enforcing contracts and protecting property.
extra: argument: Voluntary exchange only happens when both sides expect to gain, so every rule that blocks a willing trade destroys value that someone wanted.

text: Markets should set most prices and wages, but government should step in where markets clearly fail, such as monopolies, pollution, and people left with no way to earn a living.
extra: argument: Markets and governments both fail in predictable ways, so the best results come from using each where its track record is strongest.

text: Government should actively steer markets with strong regulation, a meaningful minimum wage, and taxes that share income more evenly, while leaving most production in private hands.
extra: argument: Markets reward those who already hold bargaining power, so without public rules on wages and income the gains from growth flow mainly to the people who need them least.

text: Government should direct the economy, setting key prices and wages and sharing income so that no one's living depends on the outcome of private markets.
extra: argument: Basic needs like food, housing, and work are too important to leave to a system that treats them as products sold only to those who can pay.

People are best served when they are free to make their own economic choices, and concentrated government power over the economy is a greater danger than market failures.

extra: method: Draw 100 songs at random from each decade's Billboard Hot 100 top 40, hide titles and artists, and have a panel of listeners aged 15 to 22 who do not recognize the songs rate each one; compare the average rating by decade. | validity: High | reliability: Medium | linkage: High | importance: High | strengthen: Listeners rate the randomly chosen 1970s and 1980s hits clearly higher than the randomly chosen 2010s and 2020s hits. | weaken: Listeners rate the decades about equally, or rate the recent hits higher.

method: Extend the method of Mauch and colleagues (2015) to Billboard Hot 100 recordings through 2025 and compare harmonic and timbral diversity scores for the 1970s, 1980s, 2010s and 2020s. | validity: Medium | reliability: High | linkage: Medium | importance: Medium | strengthen: Diversity in the 2010s and 2020s falls below the levels of the 1970s and 1980s. | weaken: Diversity in the 2010s and 2020s is at or above the levels of the 1970s and 1980s.

method: Use streaming-service or Luminate data broken down by listener age to measure the share of streams by listeners under 25 that go to songs released 1970 to 1989, tracked each year. | validity: Medium | reliability: Medium | linkage: Medium | importance: Medium | strengthen: Listeners under 25 give 1970s and 1980s songs a large and steady or rising share of their streams. | weaken: Listeners under 25 give 1970s and 1980s songs only a small share of their streams, falling over time.

extra: what: The two sides disagree about whether the common preference for 1970s and 1980s music comes from the music itself or from the age of the listeners who hold it. | move: A blind test in which listeners born after 2000, who did not grow up with either era, rate unlabeled hits from 1975 to 1985 and from 2015 to 2025 would go a long way toward settling it.

text: Empirical
extra: what: The two sides disagree about whether the typical hit of the 1970s and 1980s, including the forgotten ones, was better than the typical hit today, or only the survivors were. | move: Comparing random samples drawn from the full Billboard Hot 100 of each era, rather than from greatest-hits lists, would settle how much survivorship explains.

text: Values
extra: what: The two sides weigh different things as quality, with supporters stressing craft and complexity and opponents stressing variety, reach and new voices. | move: Agreeing in advance on which measures count, and how much each counts, would turn much of the argument into a question of measurement.
